3b(1).fact: Atomic nuclei and nucleons are far smaller than light wavelengths, requiring scientists to bombard targets with accelerated particle beams and measure resulting collision angles and energies to infer nuclear structure.
3b(1).misconception: Nuclear scientists observe individual protons and neutrons by placing atomic samples under high-powered optical microscopes.
3b(1).pamphlet_summary: Scouts arrange a guided tour or interview at a university physics department or national laboratory to observe radiation detection equipment and discuss nucleon scattering experiments with active researchers. The discussion explores how high-energy particle beams probe internal nuclear structures like quarks and binding forces instead of visual microscopes (p. 46).
3b(1).socratic_question: Because protons and neutrons are far too small to reflect visible light, how might shooting charged particles at an atom reveal the internal arrangement of its nucleus?

3b(2).fact: Most operational particle accelerators worldwide are compact machines deployed in hospitals and factories for cancer radiation therapy, medical isotope production, and semiconductor manufacturing.
3b(2).misconception: Particle accelerators serve only theoretical high-energy physics research and have no practical everyday applications outside advanced physics laboratories.
3b(2).pamphlet_summary: Scouts investigate three distinct accelerator architectures such as linear accelerators, cyclotrons, and synchrotrons to analyze collision experiments revealing fundamental nuclear interactions. Candidates must connect these experimental breakthroughs to practical uses including targeted cancer radiotherapy, radiopharmaceutical production, and industrial materials analysis (p. 48).
3b(2).socratic_question: Beyond smashing atoms to discover theoretical particles, in what ways do doctors and manufacturing engineers use beams of accelerated particles every day?
